data.name: Galaxy Annihilation
data.detailed_description:
Galaxy Annihilation is a shoot'em up where we need to protect the planet earth from an impending alien attack.



- 3 difficulties (easy, normal, hard).
- 31 missions.
- survival mode.
- 4 worlds.
- 15 ships.
- 12 weapons.
- 13 powerups.
- many permanent upgrades to unlock.
- 8 bosses.
- 14 achievements to unlock.
And Much More...



Keyboard and mouse
Wasd Or Arrow Keys - to Move the Spaceships.
left-click or spacebar - to shoot with the primary weapon.
right-click or E - to shoot with secondary weapon.
middle-mouse button or Q - to use the special.

Controller
Left analogue stick - to Move the spaceships.
A on gamepad - to shoot with the primary weapon.
B on gamepad - to shoot with secondary weapon.
X on gamepad - to use the special.
Right analog stick - to navigate on the menus.

reviews.review:
Galaxy Annihilation is a traditional arcade space shooter that delivers a straightforward experience built around defending Earth from an approaching alien invasion. Developed and published by Lunarhellgames, the game embraces the familiar shoot 'em up formula while introducing a respectable selection of missions, spacecraft, weapons, and upgrades. Rather than attempting to revolutionize the genre, it concentrates on accessible combat, continuous progression, and increasingly demanding encounters. Its uncomplicated premise makes it easy to approach, especially for players who enjoy classic spaceship shooters where survival depends on quick reactions, accurate shooting, and careful movement.

The core gameplay emphasizes maneuvering through hostile environments while eliminating waves of extraterrestrial enemies. Players control their spacecraft using directional inputs and have access to primary weapons, secondary attacks, and special abilities. This arrangement provides some tactical flexibility, as different offensive options can be used depending on the situation. The controls are relatively simple, allowing newcomers to understand the mechanics without extensive tutorials. However, simplicity also creates limitations. Much of the entertainment depends on how engaging the shooting feels over extended sessions, and the conventional combat structure may eventually become predictable for experienced genre enthusiasts.

One of the game's strongest selling points is its substantial collection of playable content. With 31 missions distributed across four worlds, Galaxy Annihilation provides a structured campaign that encourages gradual advancement. Three difficulty settings accommodate different skill levels, allowing beginners to enjoy a more forgiving experience while experienced players pursue greater challenges. Eight bosses introduce additional obstacles that can demand stronger equipment and more disciplined movement. The campaign's numerical variety is appealing, although the experience would benefit most from distinctive enemy behaviors and memorable mission designs. Having numerous stages is valuable, but maintaining excitement throughout them remains equally important.

Customization contributes significantly to the game's appeal. Players can access 15 spacecraft, 12 weapons, 13 power-ups, and numerous permanent upgrades. These systems create opportunities to experiment with different combat configurations and establish a sense of progression beyond simply completing missions. Unlocking additional equipment gives players tangible objectives, while permanent improvements provide incentives to continue playing. The selection is generous for a relatively modest independent title, although the actual depth depends on how noticeably each option changes combat performance. Players who appreciate collecting equipment and gradually strengthening their capabilities will likely find this aspect particularly attractive.

Beyond the campaign, survival mode provides an alternative challenge focused on endurance rather than conventional mission progression. This addition complements the arcade format by encouraging players to improve their reactions, refine their offensive strategies, and survive increasingly demanding encounters. Steam leaderboards introduce a competitive element, while 14 achievements offer further objectives for completionists. Together, these features strengthen replayability and give players reasons to return after completing the main missions. Nevertheless, their effectiveness remains closely connected to the underlying combat. Repeated encounters can become monotonous when the shooting mechanics lack sufficient variety, regardless of how many secondary objectives are available.

The presentation follows a modest science-fiction arcade direction, placing greater emphasis on gameplay functionality than narrative complexity. The alien invasion premise establishes an immediate objective without requiring elaborate storytelling or character development. This approach works reasonably well for an action-focused experience, although players searching for atmospheric world-building or a memorable storyline may find it lacking. Its relatively lightweight technical requirements are another advantage, with only 2 GB of minimum memory and approximately 150 MB of storage required. English and Italian interface support further accommodate its intended audience, although broader localization would improve accessibility.

Control flexibility is another welcome feature. Keyboard and mouse users can move with WASD or directional keys, while separate buttons handle primary fire, secondary weapons, and special attacks. Controller support provides an alternative for players who prefer analog movement and conventional gamepad inputs. Regarding Steam Deck compatibility, the game currently has an Unknown or Unverified status, with no confirmed official Verified or Playable designation. Its native SteamOS and Linux support, controller functionality, and modest hardware requirements are promising characteristics, but they do not guarantee seamless handheld operation. Players should therefore consider Steam Deck performance and interface compatibility unconfirmed until independently tested.

The game's greatest limitation is its dependence on established arcade shooter conventions. Its basic premise, combat structure, and progression systems are familiar, making it difficult to identify a defining feature that separates it from more ambitious competitors. Although the quantity of available content is commendable, the overall experience may appeal more strongly to dedicated arcade enthusiasts than to players seeking innovation. The limited number of Steam user reviews also makes it difficult to establish a reliable community consensus regarding its quality. These concerns do not necessarily diminish its entertainment potential, but they reinforce the importance of approaching it with realistic expectations.

Ultimately, Galaxy Annihilation presents a respectable independent shooting experience that prioritizes accessibility, equipment progression, and straightforward arcade entertainment. Its combination of numerous missions, multiple spacecraft, varied weapons, permanent upgrades, boss encounters, and survival challenges provides an appealing foundation for fans of traditional space combat. While its familiar design and limited narrative ambitions prevent it from standing out as an exceptional genre entry, there is enough advertised content to make it worth considering for players who appreciate uncomplicated action and collectible upgrades. It is a modest but potentially enjoyable experience that understands its intended audience without attempting to become something considerably larger.

A content-rich yet conventional arcade space shooter with accessible controls, generous customization, and worthwhile replay incentives, best suited to enthusiasts of classic extraterrestrial combat.

Rating: 6/10
